"Aadhya and Ira, the twins," people call us. They ask how we stayed close for six years at the same firm. Honestly? We started on the same day, both terrified, both given the desks next to the broken AC. That was the beginning.
When my engagement broke, Ira drove to my flat at midnight with a box of jalebis and didn't ask a single question until I was ready. When her father was in hospital in Lucknow for three weeks, I covered her client calls and sent her updates so she wouldn't miss anything.
There's a kind of friend you perform for, and a kind you don't. With Ira, I've been the girl crying in the office washroom with mascara everywhere, and she just handed me tissues and said, "Fix your face, we have a meeting in ten, you'll be brilliant."
She's the one person I can be a complete mess around. I don't have to explain myself.

qa.q: What did Ira bring when Aadhya's engagement broke?
qa.a: Ira drove to Aadhya's flat at midnight with a box of jalebis.

qa.q: Why does Aadhya say she doesn't have to explain herself with Ira?
qa.a: Aadhya feels completely safe with Ira: she can be a mess, even crying in the washroom, and Ira meets it with care, not judgement. 😊

qa.q: What habits have kept this friendship strong?
qa.a: Each shows up at the other's worst moments in practical ways, like covering calls or arriving at midnight, and neither asks the other to perform.

qa.q: What might Ira value about the friendship?
qa.a: Ira probably values that Aadhya carried her work while her father was in hospital, so she could be with family without worrying.

grounding: Shows two colleagues who started together and carried each other through a broken engagement and a parent's illness, with one able to be at her weakest without judgement.

I sit two desks away from Sarita and Vijay in the accounts team, so I've watched them for three years. They joined the same week, fresh from college, and they still order lunch from the same dhaba every Thursday.
Last winter, when Sarita's mother was ill, Vijay quietly took over her month-end files and never mentioned it in team meetings. When Vijay's girlfriend ended things, Sarita sat with him on the stairwell for most of an afternoon.
What I notice most is how different Sarita is around him. With the rest of us she's polished, careful with every word. With Vijay she'll put her head on the desk and groan, "I'm useless today," and he'll slide a chai across and say, "Useless people don't finish audits." She laughs.
I can't know what's in their heads. But she looks like someone who knows she won't be judged.

qa.q: What does Vijay slide across when Sarita says she's useless?
qa.a: Vijay slides a chai across and says, 'Useless people don't finish audits.'

qa.q: What does Sarita's change around Vijay suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests Sarita feels safe with Vijay; she drops her polished, careful manner because she trusts she won't be judged. 🙂

qa.q: What could the rest of the team learn from how these two support each other?
qa.a: Quiet, practical help, like taking over files without announcing it, builds deep trust more than big words do.

qa.q: How does the narrator see Sarita differently with Vijay than with everyone else?
qa.a: The narrator sees a polished, careful Sarita with the team and a relaxed, honest one with Vijay, while admitting not knowing what either of them thinks.

grounding: Illustrates, through a colleague's eyes, a years-long work friendship through illness and breakup in which one woman can be at her weakest without being judged.

You want to know about Kamal? Okay. I'm Gargi, and Kamal and I joined the agency the same week, four years ago, both terrified, both sitting in the corner by the broken printer.

Since then he's been there for everything. When my engagement broke off, he didn't say a word about it at the office. He just left a flask of hot soup on my desk every day for a week.

When my mother was in hospital last year, he covered my client calls without being asked and texted me every night: "Eaten?" That's all. Just "Eaten?"

I've cried in front of him in the stairwell more times than I can count. I've said stupid, bitter things. He's never once made me feel judged.

He's the person I can be at my worst around. I don't have many of those.

qa.q: What did Kamal leave on Gargi's desk after her engagement broke off?
qa.a: A flask of hot soup, every day for a week.

qa.q: How does Gargi feel about having Kamal in her life?
qa.a: Gargi feels deeply grateful and safe with him, trusting him as the person she can be at her worst around without being judged.

qa.q: Why does Kamal's kind of support work for Gargi?
qa.a: He offers small, steady practical care, like soup and a nightly "Eaten?", without questioning or gossiping.

qa.q: What might it mean to Kamal to be trusted like this?
qa.a: He may feel valued and close to Gargi, perhaps glad to be needed after starting out just as scared as she was.

grounding: Gargi describes her colleague Kamal supporting her through a broken engagement and her mother's illness, as the person she can be weakest around without judgement.

March, their first week at the bank in Kochi. Lavanya and Neelam were the only two trainees who didn't know anyone, and they ended up sharing a lunch table and complaining about the air conditioning.

November, the same year. Neelam's father had a stroke. Lavanya drove her to the hospital at midnight and sat with her in the corridor until morning, holding her bag and her phone, saying almost nothing.

February, a year on. Lavanya's boyfriend of five years ended things in a text. She came to work anyway, puffy-eyed, and went straight into the storeroom. Neelam followed, locked the door, and let her sob into her shoulder.

"I look terrible," Lavanya said.

"You look like someone who's had a terrible day," Neelam said. "That's allowed here."

Lavanya laughed, snot and all. With Neelam, she didn't have to be fine.

qa.q: Where did Lavanya sit with Neelam until morning?
qa.a: In the hospital corridor.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's laugh in the storeroom show?
qa.a: It shows she feels relieved and safe, knowing she doesn't have to pretend to be fine in front of Neelam.

qa.q: How did each of them support the other well?
qa.a: They showed up quietly in the worst moments, the hospital corridor and the storeroom, without judging or needing many words.

qa.q: How might Neelam see Lavanya after the night at the hospital?
qa.a: She likely sees Lavanya as someone she can trust completely, which may be why she follows her into the storeroom.

grounding: Over a year, colleagues Lavanya and Neelam support each other through a parent's stroke and a breakup, becoming each other's safe person at their weakest.

Beta, you asked why I still call Santosh every Sunday, though we both retired years ago. Let me tell you.

We joined the railway office in Pune the same month. I was twenty-three and new to the city. The first year, I got my heart broken by a man who didn't turn up to meet my parents. I sat at my desk pretending to type, and Santosh slid a cup of cutting chai across without saying anything. He did that every afternoon for a month.

Later, when my father was dying, Santosh took my files home and finished them, so I could sit at the hospital. He never mentioned it to our boss.

I could be a mess in front of him. Weepy, angry, even unkind. He never once looked at me like I was less.

That's why, beta. Some people are rare. I, Mahima, have had only one of those.

qa.q: What did Santosh slide across Mahima's desk every afternoon for a month?
qa.a: A cup of cutting chai.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel being able to be a mess in front of Santosh?
qa.a: She felt safe and accepted, never judged or made to feel less, which is why she still values him.

qa.q: What choice in the story shows the depth of Santosh's loyalty?
qa.a: Taking Mahima's files home when her father was dying, and never telling the boss, so she could be at the hospital.

qa.q: How might Santosh have felt about Mahima's heartbreak?
qa.a: He was probably concerned and caring, choosing quiet support with chai instead of questions.

grounding: Mahima, an elder, recalls a colleague who supported her through heartbreak and her father's dying, the person she could be weakest around without judgement.

It was 11 p.m. at the office, the air conditioning had died with the power, and the client deck was due at eight in the morning.

Elizabeth sat on the floor of the conference room with her laptop on a chair, and Shankar handed her a torch.

"Remember our first week here?" he said. "Four years ago. Neither of us knew how to use the printer."

She laughed, then went quiet. Shankar had driven her to the hospital the night her mother had surgery. He'd listened to her cry on the fire escape after her breakup, and never once said "I told you so."

"You're the only person here I can be a total mess around," she said.

"Likewise," said Shankar, sliding her a packet of biscuits. "Now. Slide nine is ugly."

By three, the deck was done. By then she was too tired to be anything but herself, and it didn't matter.

qa.q: Where did Shankar drive Elizabeth on the night of her mother's surgery?
qa.a: He drove her to the hospital.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she told Shankar he's the only person she can be a mess around?
qa.a: She felt safe and grateful, trusting him completely after years of support.

qa.q: What keeps friendships like this strong?
qa.a: Showing up in hard moments, listening without judging and working side by side, as Shankar did, builds deep trust.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel about their friendship?
qa.a: Shankar seems to value it just as much, saying 'likewise' and easing the pressure with biscuits and humour.

grounding: During a late-night deadline, two long-time colleagues show years of mutual support, where one can be at her weakest without judgement.
